title: Factors Associated with Participation in the Hide and Skin Business in Chiro Town, Ethiopia: Evidence from Binary Logistic Regression
content: Introduction: The hide and skin subsector is an important component of Ethiopia's livestock value chain, contributing to employment creation, income generation, and the supply of raw materials for the leather industry. Despite the country's substantial livestock resources, the subsector remains constrained by poor raw-material quality, limited access to financial and market services, inadequate transportation facilities, and institutional challenges. Understanding the factors associated with participation is therefore essential for strengthening the subsector and improving its contribution to local economic development. This study investigated the socioeconomic, institutional, and market-related factors associated with participation in the hide and skin business in Chiro Town, West Hararghe Zone, Oromia Regional State, Ethiopia. Methods: A quantitative cross-sectional research design was employed using 173 observations from Burqa Chiro, Caffee Araraa, and Ifaa Misooma kebeles. A census approach was reportedly applied to include all identified study units. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize respondents' characteristics and business-related conditions, while binary logistic regression was employed to identify factors associated with participation in the hide and skin business. Results: The estimated logistic regression model was statistically significant (Omnibus χ² = 180.880, df = 12, p < 0.001), with a Nagelkerke pseudo-R² of 0.915. The Hosmer–Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test was not statistically significant (χ² = 4.310, df = 8, p = 0.828). The regression results revealed that family size, access to credit, market information, livestock ownership, transportation access, training, veterinary services, and government policy and regulatory support were positively and significantly associated with participation. In contrast, age and distance to market were negatively and significantly associated with participation. Sex and educational status showed no statistically significant associations. Conclusion: Participation in the hide and skin business is associated with a combination of socioeconomic resources, institutional services, and market accessibility. Strengthening access to affordable financial services, reliable market information, transportation infrastructure, technical training, veterinary services, and supportive institutional arrangements may create a more favorable environment for business participation and value-chain development. The findings provide locally relevant evidence for policymakers and stakeholders seeking to improve the hide and skin subsector in Chiro Town. Nevertheless, the exceptionally large odds ratios and wide confidence intervals for several explanatory variables, together with uncertainty regarding the unit of analysis, necessitate further verification of the sampling frame, variable coding, and regression estimates before definitive household-level conclusions are drawn.
